mcqs.question: In a row-major matrix with cols columns, what does the address formula base + (i * cols + j) * element_size compute?
options: The number of elements in row i alone
The total number of rows in the matrix
The distance in bytes between two consecutive rows
The flat memory offset of mat[i][j], since all of row i's elements plus the first j elements of row i come before it
mcqs.explanation: i * cols counts every element in the rows before row i, and adding j moves to the correct column within row i, giving the exact flat offset of mat[i][j]. It isn't a row count, a row length, or a byte-distance between rows on its own.

mcqs.question: On a large row-major matrix, why can row-by-row traversal be noticeably faster than column-by-column traversal, even though both are O(rows·cols)?
options: Row-by-row traversal only works correctly on square matrices
Row-by-row traversal visits fewer elements in total
Column-by-column traversal has a worse Big-O complexity
Row-by-row traversal accesses memory sequentially, which is cache-friendly, while column-by-column jumps between rows and misses cache more often
mcqs.explanation: Both orders visit every element exactly once and share the same Big-O class — the real-world gap comes from cache locality: sequential access hits cache lines already loaded, while column-by-column strides across rows and misses cache repeatedly. Neither traversal order is restricted to square matrices.

mcqs.question: Implementing 90° rotation as transpose-then-reverse-each-row on an n x n matrix, what's the space complexity?
options: O(n), for one temporary row buffer
O(n log n), from sorting each row before reversing
O(1), since both the transpose and the row reversals operate on the existing matrix in place
O(n²), because a full copy of the matrix must be made first
mcqs.explanation: The transpose swaps elements across the diagonal within the existing matrix, and reversing each row swaps within that row — neither step allocates a new matrix or row buffer, so the whole rotation is O(1) extra space. Nothing here involves sorting or a full copy.

mcqs.question: Given a correct 90° clockwise rotation function, how would you produce a 270° clockwise rotation without writing a new algorithm from scratch?
options: Apply the 90° clockwise rotation three times
Apply the 90° clockwise rotation once, then transpose again
Reverse every row of the original matrix once
Apply the 90° clockwise rotation half a time, rounded up
mcqs.explanation: 270° clockwise is three applications of the 90° rotation composed together — the same primitive reused rather than a new derivation. A single row reversal or an extra transpose doesn't produce the correct 270° result.

mcqs.question: Why can't a rows x cols matrix (rows != cols) be rotated 90° truly in place using the same array's storage?
options: It's possible, just slower than the square case
It's impossible only when rows and cols are both even numbers
The rotated result has dimensions cols x rows — a different shape that literally doesn't fit in the original backing array
In-place rotation requires the matrix to contain only positive numbers
mcqs.explanation: Rotating a non-square matrix changes its dimensions, so the output can't be written back into the same array's existing shape no matter how cleverly indices are computed — the result needs O(rows·cols) new storage. This isn't about parity of dimensions or the sign of the values; it's a genuine shape mismatch.

mcqs.question: In a spiral traversal, why does the innermost ring (a single row or column) need an extra check before continuing to the next directional walk?
options: Without checking whether top/bottom or left/right have already crossed, the traversal can revisit cells already visited by an earlier walk in the same ring
Because spiral traversal doesn't work on matrices with an odd number of rows
Because the direction of traversal must reverse at the innermost ring
Because the innermost ring always has exactly one element
mcqs.explanation: If a ring has collapsed to one row or column, top and bottom (or left and right) can already be equal or crossed, so walking the remaining directions without a boundary check revisits already-visited cells or reads past the collapsed edge. Odd row counts work fine with the check in place, and the innermost ring can be a single cell, a row, or a column — not always just one element.
